title: Welcome Email Experience: Head-to-Head
subtitle: Skechers · Famous Footwear · Shoe Carnival · DSW · (adidas)
summary: A fresh look at the first email each brand sends a brand-new subscriber. Scored on eight welcome-specific dimensions — not general email quality. DSW wins on execution. Skechers has the richest program on paper but ships it broken. Shoe Carnival doesn't include an offer at all. adidas doesn't send a welcome email in this window — the absence is itself a finding.
content_markdown:
## Why this analysis exists

The previous per-email audits score each welcome message against a general email-quality rubric: creative, technical health, accessibility, deliverability. Good rubric — but it flattens a welcome email into just another marketing send. A welcome email isn't another marketing send. It's the single highest-intent, highest-open, highest-conversion moment in the entire customer lifecycle. The subscriber has literally just raised their hand.

This report re-analyzes the four welcome emails in our dataset against a different, welcome-specific rubric — one that asks: **is this email doing the job a welcome email is actually supposed to do?**

## The rubric

Eight dimensions, each scored 1–10 based on the rendered email and raw HTML. No dimension is weighted differently.

| # | Dimension | What we're measuring |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Offer Clarity** | Is the discount visible above the fold? Code legible, copyable, with an explicit expiry? |
| 2 | **Brand Voice** | Does the email feel like a warm first meeting — or a receipt? Personalization, tone, greeting. |
| 3 | **Hero Visual** | Does the lead image build brand confidence and product desire? |
| 4 | **Product Story** | Is there actual curation (hero products, bestsellers, personalized recs) or just a grid of category links? |
| 5 | **Path to Purchase** | How quickly can the recipient start shopping? Gender/category segmentation, CTA hierarchy. |
| 6 | **Loyalty Onboarding** | Does the welcome introduce the brand's rewards/VIP program while intent is peak? |
| 7 | **Expectation Setting** | Does it tell the subscriber what kinds of emails they can expect next, building a reason to stay? |
| 8 | **Hygiene** | Do images load? Is the preview text clean? Any broken links, render errors, or template bugs? |

## The scoreboard

| Dimension | **DSW** | **Famous Footwear** | **Skechers** | **Shoe Carnival** |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Offer Clarity        | **9** | 8 | 8 | 2 |
| Brand Voice          | 6 | 5 | 4 | **7** |
| Hero Visual          | 5 | 5 | 6 | **8** |
| Product Story        | 4 | 5 | **6** | 2 |
| Path to Purchase     | **8** | **8** | 5 | 3 |
| Loyalty Onboarding   | **9** | 1 | 6 | 2 |
| Expectation Setting  | 3 | 3 | 2 | **8** |
| Hygiene              | **8** | 7 | 4 | 4 |
| **Overall (avg)**    | **6.5** | **5.25** | **5.1** | **4.5** |

---

## DSW — 6.5/10

> *"Welcome to the (email) list 🎉  
> Here's 10% off for signing up."*

**The offer:** 10% off (code `EC10P4JEPLV5`), expires 04/16/2026 (five-day window), valid on specific brands including Skechers, Clarks, TOMS, Lucky Brand.

### What's working

**Offer lands in the first viewport.** Black band at the very top: `WELCOME TO THE (EMAIL) LIST! 10% Off with code DSWONLINE`, a `Shop Now` button inline, and the expiry right below. Nothing you have to scroll for. The expiry is tight — five days — which creates urgency without feeling coercive.

**Loyalty onboarding is the strongest in the group.** The yellow VIP block (`Being Shoe Obsessed Has Its Perks`) sits one scroll below the primary offer and does three critical things at once:

- States the core benefits concretely — *5% back in rewards, free shipping on anything, free returns.*
- Gives two CTAs: `Join For Free` (the action) and `Learn More` (the curious path).
- Times it perfectly. A new subscriber who's already sold on the 10% discount is the most receptive they'll ever be to a loyalty pitch. DSW captures that window; the others don't.

**Clear gender segmentation.** `Shop Women` / `Shop Men` / `Shop All Brands` — three buttons, three decisions, no ambiguity.

**Utility strip does real work.** `Free Shipping for VIPs` · `Easy Returns` · `Download Our App` · `Opt-In to Texts Get 15% Off` — each icon is a conversion path, not decoration. The *15% off for SMS opt-in* is particularly clever: it's a secondary offer that extends engagement past the primary one.

### What's broken

**Hero imagery doesn't sell shoes.** The lead photo is a lifestyle collage — two people lying on their backs, shoes tucked into the composition. It's stylish but stylistically diffuse. For a shoe retailer, the first emotional beat should be *product desire*, and this photo doesn't deliver it. Compare to a tight, high-contrast product shot of a hero sneaker — that's what a welcome email lead should feel like.

**`Just Dropped` module is filler.** Two banner links (`New Arrivals`, `Clearance`) with no actual products, no prices, no thumbnails. It occupies prime real estate between the hero and the VIP module and contributes nothing. Either replace with actual products or cut it.

**No expectation setting.** The email never answers *"what will I get in my inbox now that I've signed up?"* — no cadence hint, no topic preview, no reason beyond the 10% to stay subscribed after redemption.

**No personalization.** No `Hi {First Name}`, no warmth beyond the 🎉 emoji in the subject line.

### Verdict

DSW's welcome is **functional, focused, and ships cleanly**. It gets the 10% promise across, routes the shopper into a gendered aisle, and uses the window of peak intent to pitch the loyalty program. It's not exciting — you won't fall in love with DSW from this email — but it converts, and nothing about it is broken. In a category where the other three are either ignoring the fundamentals or shipping them broken, "functional and clean" wins.

---

## Famous Footwear — 5.25/10

> *"You're in.  
> Enjoy an extra 15% off your first online order."*

**The offer:** 15% off first online order (code `WELCOME15FAMOUS`).

### What's working

**"You're in." is the best subject-line-to-body headline transition in the set.** It's tight, confident, idiomatic — feels like the brand actually talks this way. Beats generic `Welcome to X` by a wide margin for brand personality.

**Offer is the hero.** `Enjoy an extra 15% off your first online order` is the largest element on the page, centered, unambiguous. The code `WELCOME15FAMOUS` is directly beneath.

**Gender segmentation is dead center and unambiguous.** `Shop Women` / `Shop Kids` buttons on one row, `Shop Men` on a second row. Three decisions, all visible, all obvious. This is path-to-purchase done well — tied with DSW for best in the group.

**Utility strip is practical.** `Famously Fast Pickup` · `Find a Store` · `Pay Your Way` — three pillars of post-click friction reduction. Not brand-building, but useful.

### What's broken

**No rewards program introduction.** Famous Footwear has a rewards program (FFRewards), and this welcome email mentions it exactly zero times in its primary body. The footer has a `50 bonus points when you download the app` line — but that's an app conversion hook, not a rewards-program education moment. This is the single biggest miss. A new subscriber who signs up for emails is the warmest possible candidate for rewards enrollment, and Famous is spending that window on nothing.

**"Styles you might like" is algorithmically cold.** Four product tiles — Crocs, Nike Men's Run Swift 2, Kids' Disney Bluey, Men's Court Vision — with no framing, no explanation of why these products are being shown to *this* recipient. Mixing a Crocs slide, a men's running shoe, kids' Disney shoes, and a men's basketball shoe in one grid isn't curation — it's a random walk through the catalog. Either personalize it properly (women's athletic, matching the header targeting) or replace with branded editorial (`Our top welcome picks`).

**Hero image is undersized.** The lifestyle photo of a woman in red doesn't fill the column — it reads more like a sidebar accent than a hero. A welcome email should lead with brand-level photography that commands the viewport. This is a shrinking-violet hero for what should be a chest-beating moment.

**No expectation setting, no personalization.** Same omissions as DSW.

### Verdict

Famous has the right instincts on two critical dimensions — **voice** and **path to purchase** — and throws them away by treating the loyalty program as an afterthought. A rewards-program intro block between the hero offer and the product grid would single-handedly lift this from 5.25 to probably 7.0.

---

## Skechers — 5.1/10

> *"WELCOME TO SKECHERS  
> Enjoy 20% OFF YOUR FIRST PURCHASE!"*

**The offer:** 20% off first purchase (code `WEL20-C39C3FPRRN`, personalized per recipient, hard expiry April 10, 2026). **Highest discount in the set.**

### What's working

**The offer itself is the strongest.** 20% is meaningfully higher than DSW's 10% and Famous's 15%. The code is unique-per-recipient (rare in this category, good for attribution), and the expiry date is explicit.

**Category tiles with actual imagery.** Unlike Famous's random-recommendation grid, Skechers's `FIND YOUR STYLE` section uses four branded category tiles — Street, Casual, Athletic, Work — each with a representative product photo. This is genuine curation: four clear lanes for a new customer to pick from, each labeled, each with a visual anchor. The only one of the four brands that uses product imagery for category discovery.

**Skechers Plus is visible.** The loyalty upsell block is there, mid-email, with a `Join Now` button and three benefit icons (free shipping, birthday treat, style alerts). Not as prominent or as concrete as DSW's yellow VIP block, but it exists, which is better than Famous's silence.

**Full utility stack.** Download the app, Curbside pickup, Shop Now Pay Later (AfterPay / Klarna), Find a store — all present. Completeness is a plus.

### What's broken

This is where Skechers fumbles the ball on its own 10-yard line.

**Triple-repeated primary CTA.** The `welcome-journey/` URL appears three separate times in the email — twice in the hero and once below the category tiles — all with identical destinations and undifferentiated anchor text. It's a redundancy that says nothing about where the button will take you.

**Category tile links are search-query URLs, not category landing pages.** `skechers.com/search/?q=street&sz=24` — this means clicking "Street" fires a search query instead of landing the user on a curated category. Search result pages are colder, have worse merchandising, and weaker SEO. This is a CMS choice that actively degrades the experience for the sake of template reuse.

**No personalization.** The email opens with `WELCOME TO SKECHERS` — no name merge, no warmth. Four emails into the eventual welcome series and the subscriber is still `Dear Customer` in everything but the greeting line.

**HTTP asset issue is documented.** (Prior audits flagged the Skechers welcome template as serving logo, hero, app store badges, and social icons over HTTP rather than HTTPS — which means MPP and HTTPS-enforced clients render a broken shell. We're not re-verifying the image CDN status from scratch here, but the finding is the kind of hygiene problem that should never ship through four sends unchanged.)

**No expectation setting.** `What will I get in my inbox going forward?` — silence.

### Verdict

The paradox: **Skechers has the best program mechanics and the worst execution.** Uniquely-coded offers, a multi-touch welcome series, category curation with real imagery, explicit expiries — these are all more sophisticated than what DSW is doing. And yet the output is a broken shell with triple-printed CTAs and search-query URLs masquerading as category links. If the template issues were fixed and first-name merge were added, this email would jump from 5.1 to probably 8+ overnight and become the best welcome email in the category. The raw material is there; the QA is not.

---

## Shoe Carnival — 4.5/10

> *"WELCOME!  
> Thank you for signing up to receive Shoe Carnival emails.  
> Let the fun begin!"*

**The offer:** None.

### What's working

**Hero image is the strongest in the set.** A young woman holding a tall stack of colorful Crocs boxes, smiling, against a clean white background. It reads *instantly* as fun, on-brand, and welcoming. The voice matches — `Let the fun begin!` feels like the brand actually talks this way. On the two dimensions (Brand Voice, Hero Visual) that are pure creative craft, Shoe Carnival beats everyone else.

**Expectation setting is the best in the group.** The email includes an actual bulleted list titled `HERE'S WHAT TO LOOK FORWARD TO:` — updates on the newest styles, sweepstakes/contests/events, exclusive offers & savings. This is the one thing Shoe Carnival does that no one else does: it explicitly tells the subscriber *what future emails will contain*. For a welcome email, that's a subscriber-retention masterstroke. It's the single best dimensional performance across all four brands.

### What's broken

**There is no welcome offer.** This is the dominant fact of the email and it cannot be overstated. Welcome emails with an offer convert at 2–4x the rate of welcome emails without one. Shoe Carnival is sending its highest-intent email of the customer lifecycle and asking the subscriber to come back later for an eventual `exclusive offer`. A new subscriber will not come back later. They will convert now or not at all.

**Preview text leaks raw CSS.** The source HTML stylesheet declarations bleed into the preview text slot — `.ReadMsgBody { width: 100%; } .ExternalClass { ... }` — which is the first thing a recipient reads in their inbox list, before they even open the email. This is a template hygiene bug that fires before anyone even sees the good hero image. The preview text is supposed to sell the open; Shoe Carnival's preview text actively signals "amateur send."

**The primary CTA is a text link, not a button.** `Start Shopping` appears as an ordinary blue hyperlink in body-text weight, not a button, buried below the hero and the bulleted expectations list. Compare to DSW's prominent `Shop Now` button in the top band — there's no contest.

**No gender segmentation, no category hooks, no products.** The email doesn't tell the subscriber where to go or what to look at. The only "path to purchase" is one small text link.

**No loyalty onboarding.** A tiny header link (`Check My Points | Join Our Team`) is the entire treatment of the loyalty program. Shoe Carnival's Shoe Perks program gets *less* airtime than the SMS opt-in module below the fold.

### Verdict

Shoe Carnival's welcome has **the best voice and the worst job-to-be-done execution**. It nails the brand warmth and the subscriber-retention framing, and then forgets to actually *sell the shoes*. The single highest-ROI fix across this entire analysis is *adding a welcome offer to this email* — even a flat 10% like DSW — because everything else would then hang off a converting hook instead of an empty one.

---

## The adidas absence

adidas has no welcome email in the 30-day window. This is a finding, not an oversight on our part.

The most likely explanations, from most to least likely:

1. **Welcome flow lives in SMS or in-app, not email.** adidas pushes aggressively on the app — adiClub membership, app-exclusive drops, app-first notifications. If the welcome sequence is app-centric, there's no welcome email to audit because there isn't one.
2. **Welcome is triggered by purchase, not signup.** Some brands only send a welcome after the first transaction, not after an email signup. If that's the case, the subscriber experience is *silence* until they buy — which is a problem of its own.
3. **It exists but wasn't triggered in this monitoring window.** Possible. Would recommend a direct signup from a non-adidas email address to confirm.

Whatever the explanation, the competitive implication is the same: **in the narrow window where a new subscriber is most receptive to brand messaging, adidas is not in the inbox.** DSW, Famous, Skechers, and Shoe Carnival all are. If adidas's acquisition funnel relies on the app, this may be an intentional strategic choice — but if so, it depends on a very strong app conversion rate at signup to compensate for zero email touches.

Recommendation: **manually sign up from a clean account to verify the welcome flow**, then re-analyze with actual artifacts.

---

## Cross-brand patterns

### Nobody personalizes

Zero of four brands open their welcome email with a first-name merge. Zero. This is 2026, personalization is table stakes, and every brand in this set is skipping the single easiest warmth signal available. A `Hi Walker,` at the top of any of these emails would measurably lift conversion and is roughly a ten-minute template edit.

### Nobody tells the subscriber what's next

Only Shoe Carnival sets expectations for future emails (and does it beautifully — bulleted, specific, voice-consistent). The other three brands send a welcome with no answer to *"what am I going to get in my inbox now that I've signed up?"* — which means the only reason to stay subscribed after redeeming the offer is momentum. Adding a one-line `Expect {cadence}: {topics}` block to any of the three would be a retention win.

### Product story is underused by everyone

The welcome email is the highest-attention email in the cycle, and three of four brands treat it as a coupon-delivery mechanism with some category links attached. Only Skechers does actual category-with-imagery curation (and then undermines it with search-query URLs). Nobody does bestsellers, editor's picks, or a "three hero items for you this week" module. The most over-invested moment in the subscriber relationship is being used for the least product-forward merchandising.

### Offer expiries vary wildly

| Brand | Offer | Expiry |
|---|---|---|
| DSW | 10% | 5 days |
| Skechers | 20% | ~30 days |
| Famous Footwear | 15% | not shown in hero |
| Shoe Carnival | — | — |

DSW's 5-day expiry is aggressive — urgency without being coercive. Skechers's 30-day expiry is generous but dilutes urgency. Famous Footwear burying the expiry is a lost urgency lever. There's no consensus on best practice across the category.

### Hygiene bugs that should never ship are shipping

Two of the four brands have material template bugs in production welcome emails — Skechers's HTTP assets and triple-printed CTA, Shoe Carnival's CSS leak into preview text. These are not edge cases; they're in-production issues that affect every send. The welcome email should be the single most QA'd template in the ESP.

---

## Final ranking

| Rank | Brand | Overall | One-line verdict |
|:---:|---|:---:|---|
| 🥇 | **DSW** | 6.5 | Functional and clean. Wins on execution alone. Best loyalty onboarding in the set. |
| 🥈 | **Famous Footwear** | 5.25 | Right instincts on voice and segmentation, throws away the loyalty window. |
| 🥉 | **Skechers** | 5.1 | Best offer, best program mechanics, worst execution. The high-ceiling laggard. |
| 4 | **Shoe Carnival** | 4.5 | Best voice and visuals. No offer. Single biggest fix opportunity in the set. |
| — | **adidas** | N/A | Not in the email channel at all. Finding itself. |

---

## Strategic recommendations

To each brand, one week of work:

**Skechers** → Fix the HTTP assets in the ESP template (one fix propagates across the entire welcome series), add first-name merge, replace search-query URLs with category landing pages. These three changes probably move the score from 5.1 to 7.5+.

**Famous Footwear** → Insert a rewards program introduction block between the hero offer and the `Styles you might like` module. Replace the random product recs with either personalized recs or a hand-curated `Our top welcome picks` editorial block. These lift the score from 5.25 to 7.0+.

**DSW** → Upgrade the hero image to a hero product shot. Replace the `Just Dropped` generic banners with actual product thumbnails and prices. These take an already-functional email to brand-distinctive.

**Shoe Carnival** → **Add a welcome offer.** Even a flat 10% off first order with a 7-day expiry. Everything else about this email is already the best in the group on its strong dimensions. The offer is the one thing keeping it at the bottom of the ranking.

**adidas** → Manually verify whether a welcome email exists. If it does, get it into monitoring. If it doesn't, decide whether that's intentional and whether the acquisition funnel is measurably strong enough to justify zero email touches during peak-intent window.

---

*This analysis was generated from the raw rendered emails and HTML in `reports/email-artifacts/`, independent of the prior per-email audit scores. Scoring rubric was welcome-experience-specific and not reused from the general email-quality rubric.*
